summary: Summarizes the security properties of RSVP, the protocol used to reserve network resources. The analysis aims to build on earlier work and to record what was learned from past security activities around RSVP, and it is informational rather than a new specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP is the protocol a computer uses to ask for guaranteed bandwidth before it sends data. This memo reviews the security that RSVP already has, and points out where it is missing, such as a way to set up keys and any encryption of the messages.

questions: what does the rsvp integrity object protect
how does rsvp authenticate a user
subtitle: A survey of what RSVP's own security machinery protects, and the places it falls short.

tldr.problem: RSVP was the first quality-of-service signalling protocol with any security in it, but its security was scattered across several documents and its weaknesses were not written down anywhere.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the INTEGRITY object that protects each hop, the way user identity is carried in a policy element, the handshake that recovers a lost sequence number, and then works through the first hop, the next hop and the last hop.
tldr.outcome: The conclusion is that RSVP should be treated as a building block that has to be adapted to a given architecture, with a list of the places where the protocol needs work, chiefly key management and confidentiality.

today: RFC 4230 is an Informational memo published in December 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a survey rather than a specification: it says so itself, and its list of issues that deserve improvement is the main result.

sections.title: Why This Survey Exists
sections.content:
As the work of the NSIS working group began, concerns about security and its implications for the design of a signalling protocol were raised. Understanding the security properties and available options of RSVP requires reading a number of documents, and this one summarizes them. It is part of the wider process of analysing other signalling protocols and learning from their design, and it is meant to be a starting point for further discussion.

The document sets out its own vocabulary first, and one term in it does most of the work. RSVP's security relies on optional hop-by-hop protection using the built-in INTEGRITY object, and there are also policy-aware nodes that understand the POLICY_DATA element, which carries a second INTEGRITY object of its own. Because each incoming request is assumed to be authenticated, integrity protected and replay protected, and each router is assumed to behave as expected, a message that travels through a chain of routers is protected along the way. But that means the protection is no better than the weakest link in the chain, and one malicious router can modify messages and mount attacks that have nothing to do with quality of service. Edge devices, where end users are attached, are the most likely to be attacked, and a provider may choose not to use RSVP's own security inside its core network because something else is deployed there.

The document also separates two ideas that are easy to confuse. Host identity is carried by the INTEGRITY object in the RSVP message; user identity is carried inside the POLICY_DATA element. Because the two use different mechanisms, user-based and host-based security are covered separately. The term hop is used for a neighbouring RSVP node, which is not the same thing as an IP hop: two neighbouring RSVP nodes may be more than one IP hop apart.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo exists because the security of RSVP was spread across several documents and nobody had put the whole picture in one place. It also warns that RSVP protects each hop separately, so the safety of a message is only as good as the weakest router on its path.

sections.title: The RSVP INTEGRITY Object
sections.content:
The RSVP INTEGRITY object is the main component of RSVP's security. It provides integrity and replay protection for the content of a signalling message between two RSVP routers or between a router and a host, and it also authenticates where the data came from. It has four parts. The flags field has one defined flag, the Handshake Flag, which says the sender is willing to answer an Integrity Challenge; it can be seen as a negotiation capability carried inside every INTEGRITY object.

The key identifier selects the key used to check the keyed message digest, so it must be unique for the sender. It has a fixed length of 48 bits, and its generation is mostly up to the local host; the document assumes it is a keyed hash over a number of fields, unique when more than one security association runs in parallel between two hosts. A receiving system identifies the security association from the key identifier together with the sender's IP address, taken from the RSVP_HOP object or from the packet's source address if there is no such object.

The sequence number is 64 bits long and its starting value can be chosen arbitrarily. The length was chosen so it would not be exhausted during the life of a security association. To tell a new message from a replayed one, it must increase monotonically for every message, modulo 2^64, and the receiver accepts only numbers larger than the previous one. The process starts by handshaking and agreeing on an initial sequence number; without such a handshake the initial value has to be part of establishing the security association. Because delivery in order is not guaranteed, the receiver also needs a fixed-size window around the last sequence number to allow for out-of-order delivery.

The keyed message digest is what actually protects the message. The digest field is set to zero and a keyed hash is computed over the entire RSVP packet. The field is variable in length but must be a multiple of four octets; with HMAC-MD5 the output is 16 bytes long. HMAC-MD5 is required for an RSVP implementation, though other hash algorithms such as SHA-1 may also be supported. The key comes from a pre-shared secret, either distributed by hand or produced by a key management protocol, but no such protocol is specified here and no key length is given; the document suggests HMAC-MD5 keys of 128 bits and SHA-1 keys of 160 bits, as in IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The INTEGRITY object is a small box inside every RSVP message. It names the key to check with, carries a counter that must always go up so replays are spotted, and holds a checksum over the whole message. The counter is 64 bits, the key name is 48 bits, and the checksum uses HMAC-MD5 by default.

sections.title: User Identity, Credentials And Key Management
sections.content:
On top of host authentication, RSVP can carry a user identity. A policy element called AUTH_DATA, contained in the POLICY_DATA object, is created by the RSVP daemon on the user's host and sent inside the RSVP message. Policy decision points then use the information in it to authenticate the user and to run policy-based admission control; the policy element is processed at each hop and replaced with a new one for forwarding. The AUTH_DATA object holds information for identifying users and applications together with credentials for those identities. Its main purpose seems to be policy-based admission control rather than authentication and key management, and one AUTH_DATA object may hold more than one authentication attribute.

Two kinds of attribute are defined. The policy locator is an X.500 distinguished name used to find policy information for a user or application, in four forms: ASCII and Unicode representations of the identity, and two encrypted forms, encrypted either with the Kerberos session key or with the private key of the user's digital certificate, that is, digitally signed. If identity confidentiality is wanted, the policy locator has to be encrypted with the recipient's public key. The credentials come in five defined types: an identity encoded as an ASCII string, an identity encoded as a Unicode string, a Kerberos V5 session ticket, an X.509 version 3 certificate, and a PGP certificate. The first two carry only a plaintext string, so they give no cryptographic user authentication, though they can still be protected by the surrounding INTEGRITY objects, and they are useful for identifying applications for admission control.

Key management is assumed rather than specified. Most of the security associations needed for RSVP are assumed to exist already, so key management was done in advance, with manual key distribution as the fallback; an implementation must support it, and manual deletion of security associations must be possible, key storage must survive a restart, and each key must have its own lifetime and key identifier. When several associations with different lifetimes are active at once, a key engine is more appropriate than a plaintext file, and during an overlap the sender and receiver may hold more than one active key.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP can also carry the identity of the person or program asking for bandwidth, inside a policy element, so that a decision point can check who is asking before granting it. The credentials can be Kerberos tickets or certificates. But nothing in RSVP sets the keys up; they have to be there already.

sections.title: The Integrity Handshake
sections.content:
The Integrity Handshake was designed to let a crashed or restarted host obtain the latest valid challenge value stored at the receiving host. Because there is no key management, two messages must never use the same sequence number with the same key. A host stores the latest sequence number of a cryptographically verified message, so if it crashes and loses its sequence numbers, an adversary can replay eavesdropped packets. A genuine message from the real sender with a new sequence number would let the host update its stored value and stop further replays. With a steady flow of RSVP-protected messages between two hosts, an attacker may find it hard to inject old messages, because new authenticated messages with higher sequence numbers arrive and are stored immediately.

The handshake has two messages. Node A, having recovered from a synchronisation failure, sends an Integrity Challenge, which carries a common header and a challenge made of a key identifier and a challenge cookie; the cookie is suggested to be an MD5 hash of a local secret and a timestamp. Node B replies with an Integrity Response, which carries the common header, the INTEGRITY object and the challenge again, so the cookie is echoed. The challenge message itself is not protected with an INTEGRITY object, which was done to avoid problems when both parties do not have a valid starting sequence number. Using the handshake is recommended, though it is not mandatory, because it may not be needed in every network environment.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router restarts and forgets its sequence counter, an attacker could replay old messages. The handshake is the fix: one side asks for a cookie, the other sends it back inside a properly signed message, and the counter is back in step.

sections.title: Where RSVP Falls Short
sections.content:
The first hop is the hardest to secure, because the requirements differ and there is no trust relationship yet. An end host starting RSVP signalling has to find out whether the network supports it, which node supports it, which node it must authenticate to, which security mechanisms and algorithms are used, where the keys and security associations should come from, and whether a security association has to be established at all. RSVP as specified today is used as a building block, so these questions have to be answered as part of overall architectural choices. Without answers, an end host roaming to an unknown network cannot make ad hoc RSVP calls, and RSVP supports no negotiation of security mechanisms and algorithms.

The next hop problem arises because the next RSVP node along the path is usually assumed to be known, and knowing it matters because the right key has to be selected for the INTEGRITY object. If a node assumes the message will travel to node C but it actually reaches node B, possibly through a router that cannot verify its integrity, the processing failure returns a PathErr message to the sender. That error message names the node that recognised the error, and the original sender can use it to pick a different security association or establish one, though one may not be available.

The last hop has its own issues, and the document also covers how RSVP-protected data traffic and end-to-end security interact, and how to authorize a request. All of this illustrates the shortcomings of RSVP with respect to security.
sections.plainLanguage: The weakest points are the ends of the path. At the first hop the host knows nothing about the network, and in the middle a router may guess wrongly about which router comes next, so the wrong key is used and the message bounces back as an error.

sections.title: Conclusions And What Should Change
sections.content:
RSVP was the first quality-of-service signalling protocol to offer any security protection, but whether it is appropriate depends heavily on where it is deployed. RSVP as specified should be seen as a building block that has to be adapted to a given architecture. The document says it cannot be read as a pass or fail evaluation, and that it is not a complete description of all the security issues: RSVP extensions, multicast and traffic analysis are not covered, and the interaction with mobility protocols needs more work.

It also notes what experience has shown. Some credential types have been accepted more widely than others. Kerberos is integrated into many IETF protocols today, while public-key authentication is still considered too heavy, computationally and in bandwidth terms, for per-flow signalling, and the focus on denial of service attacks makes the demands on public-key design higher still.

The list of issues that deserve improvement is long. Discovery and signalling message delivery should be separated, and some in-path discovery mechanism is needed because neighbouring RSVP-aware nodes may not know each other. Addressing for signalling messages should be hop by hop. Standard security protocols such as IPsec, TLS or CMS should be used wherever possible, with authentication and key exchange separated from message protection, because relying on manually configured keys between neighbouring RSVP nodes is insufficient. Confidentiality protection is missing and should be added, since protocol designers can seldom foresee every environment, so users should be able to select from a full range of security services. Parameter and mechanism negotiation should be provided, and a protected message should be recognizable from a flag in the header. Authorization and charging should be better integrated into the base protocol, and data origin authentication should not be provided by non-RSVP nodes such as the policy decision point, because that procedure could be accomplished by entity authentication during the authentication and key exchange phase instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo's verdict is that RSVP is a building block, not a finished security design. The biggest gaps are the lack of any way to negotiate or set up keys, and the fact that RSVP messages are not encrypted at all.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS OF THE RSVP INTEGRITY OBJECT (RFC 4230 SECTION 3.1)

items.title: Handshake flag
items.text: Says the sender will answer an Integrity Challenge, so a restarting host can recover the latest sequence number.

items.title: Key identifier
items.text: A 48-bit value that selects the key used to check the digest. It must be unique for the sender.

items.title: Sequence number
items.text: A 64-bit counter that must increase for every message, so the receiver can spot a replay.

items.title: Keyed message digest
items.text: A keyed hash over the whole RSVP packet, computed with the digest field set to zero first. HMAC-MD5 is required, and its output is 16 bytes.

items.desc: User or application identity encoded as an ASCII string.

items.desc: User or application identity encoded as a Unicode string.

messages.label: Integrity Challenge
messages.note: Carries a key identifier and a challenge cookie. It is not protected with an INTEGRITY object.

messages.label: Integrity Response
messages.note: Echoes the cookie and adds the INTEGRITY object.
